opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that result, the Geirhos et al. finding that ImageNet-trained CNNs are strongly texture-biased, is really instructive, but maybe not in the way people sometimes take it.

The naive reading is "the model is cheating" or "it hasn't really learned what a cat is." I'd frame it differently. The model is doing exactly what we asked: minimizing loss on a particular data distribution. On ImageNet, texture is a highly predictive and computationally cheap feature. If you can tell a tabby from a golden retriever by fur pattern, you don't need to build an elaborate shape representation to get the label right. Gradient descent finds the simplest features that work, and texture is lower-hanging fruit than global shape.

So I see it as a statement about the data and the inductive biases of the architecture, not a failure of learning per se. Humans are shape-biased partly because our training distribution is so different. We see objects move, rotate, and get occluded. We interact with them physically. Shape is the invariant that matters for us. Static, curated photos don't put the same pressure on a network.

The deeper lesson for me is that benchmark accuracy underdetermines the internal mechanism. Two models can hit the same top-1 accuracy while computing very different things inside, and you only find out when you shift the distribution, like with the style-transfer cue-conflict images, where the texture says "elephant" and the shape says "cat." That's why I care about interpretability. If we want to know whether a model will generalize the way we want, we have to look at what features it's actually using, not just its score on an i.i.d. test set.

It's also encouraging, in a sense. When people trained on Stylized-ImageNet, which breaks the texture shortcut, the models became more shape-biased and more robust. So these biases aren't fixed. They respond to the data, and that gives us levers. The same principle applies to language models: if we understand which shortcuts the training distribution rewards, we can reason about and shape what the model ends up representing.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark accuracy underdetermines a model’s internal mechanism and that an i.i.d. test score does not reveal which features it uses, communicating that benchmark performance alone may be inadequate.

r002.rationale: The response discusses shape bias and generalization but does not mention autonomous robots or say they need vision systems with stronger shape bias.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think it's a scandal. I think it tells us something about the task, and something about our own assumptions, more than it tells us the model is "cheating."

Textures are legitimately predictive. If you look at ImageNet, the texture of fur, scales, or bark really does carry a lot of information about the label. The network is doing exactly what you asked, which is minimizing loss on that distribution, and it found the cheapest, most reliable features that do the job. There's a kind of simplicity bias at work. Convolutional networks, especially with small receptive fields early on, find local statistics easier to pick up than global shape, which requires integrating information across the whole image. So you get texture first, and shape only if the data forces you to.

Where it becomes a problem is the gap between the benchmark and what we actually care about. We implicitly want "recognizes a cat the way a human does," but we wrote down "gets the right label on these held-out images." Those come apart under distribution shift, and texture bias is one of the clearest cases of that. Style transfer the cat into elephant skin and the model says elephant, and a person says cat with a weird texture.

I'd push back on framing this as the model being wrong, though. The human shape bias is also just a prior, one that came from embodiment and interacting with objects, where shape is what matters for grasping and predicting physics. A disembodied classifier has no reason to inherit that. If you want shape bias, you have to make the training signal demand it, with stylized data, augmentation, or different architectures. And the results there suggest the model is perfectly capable of learning shape. It just wasn't incentivized to.

So the lesson I draw is less "deep learning is brittle" and more "benchmarks underspecify what we want." It's the same lesson that shows up everywhere in alignment. The optimizer finds the feature that most cheaply satisfies the proxy, and if the proxy doesn't distinguish the behavior you want from the one you don't, you shouldn't be surprised when you get the cheap one.

r001.rationale: It says benchmark performance can reflect an underspecified proxy that rewards texture cues rather than the desired recognition behavior.

r002.rationale: It discusses human embodiment and ways to encourage shape bias, but does not say autonomous robots likely need stronger shape bias than typical CNNs.

astra-6.text:
I think it shows that doing well on a benchmark doesn’t uniquely determine how a model solves the task. If texture reliably predicts the label, then a classifier can get very good results by using texture. The training objective doesn’t specify that it should recognize objects through shape, or use the same cues a human would.

That doesn’t mean it hasn’t learned anything real. Texture is a useful feature of the world. But it does limit what we can infer from its accuracy. If we want to know whether it relies on shape, we need examples where shape and texture point toward different answers. And whether that reliance is a problem depends on where we deploy it: will those texture cues remain reliable?

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark accuracy does not reveal which cues the classifier uses and notes that accuracy has limits, but it does not say the benchmarks themselves may be inadequate.

r002.rationale: The response discusses deployment reliability generally but does not mention autonomous robots or argue that they need systems with a stronger shape bias than typical CNNs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it shows that doing well on a benchmark doesn’t necessarily mean a model has learned the same way of solving the task that we have. Texture can be a very useful signal: if the training and test sets both reward it, there’s no particular reason for the classifier to prefer shape.

I’d be careful, though, about concluding that it isn’t really recognizing objects. Humans use texture too. The more interesting question is whether that strategy holds up when you change the relationship between texture and object identity. If you give it something with the shape of a cat and the texture of an elephant, what does it do? That helps reveal what the benchmark score alone leaves ambiguous.

So I’d interpret it as evidence about the model’s inductive biases and the data distribution, and as a reason to test generalization more carefully.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark performance can leave the model’s strategy ambiguous and calls for testing generalization more carefully, conveying that the benchmark may not adequately measure shape-based recognition.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss autonomous robots or say they need vision systems with a stronger shape bias than typical CNNs.
